market_context: United States; Medjool dates and unsweetened raisins
title: Dates vs. raisins: sugar, fiber and calories

seo.title: Dates vs. raisins: sugar, fiber and calories compared
seo.meta_description: Two concentrated dried fruits, but not identical. Compare Medjool dates and raisins per 100 g and per 30 g for sugar, fiber and calories.
seo.search_intent: Compare dates with raisins nutritionally, especially sugar, fiber, calories and realistic serving sizes.

excerpt: Dates and raisins are both concentrated dried fruits. Per 100 g, Medjools have about 277 calories, 66–67 g of sugars and 6.7 g of fiber; raisins have roughly 299 calories, 59 g of sugars and 3.7 g of fiber. In a 30-g serving, that is about 83 calories and 20 g of sugars for dates versus 90 calories and 18 g for raisins. Dates provide more fiber; raisins are not automatically higher in sugar by weight.
content_html:
Dates and raisins often occupy the same mental category: very sweet dried fruit that is easy to snack on. That is accurate, but it hides a surprise. Raisins are not necessarily higher in sugar per 100 g than Medjool dates, even though both taste intensely sweet.

Start with the 100-gram comparison

USDA reference values put Medjools at about 277 calories, 66–67 g of sugars, and 6.7 g of fiber per 100 g. Unsweetened raisins provide roughly 299 calories, 59 g of sugars, and 3.7 g of fiber per 100 g.

Per 100 gMedjool datesRaisins
Energy≈277 kcal≈299 kcal
Sugars≈66–67 g≈59 g
Fiber≈6.7 g≈3.7 g
Potassium≈696 mg≈749 mg

Dates stand out for fiber: 6.7 g versus 3.7 g per 100 g. Raisins provide about 22 more calories per 100 g, while potassium is close—roughly 749 mg in raisins versus 696 mg in Medjools.

A 30-gram serving makes the gap smaller

Thirty grams of Medjool dates contains about 83 calories, 20 g of sugars, and 2.0 g of fiber. The same 30 g of raisins provides about 90 calories, 18 g of sugars, and 1.1 g of fiber.

A 7-calorie gap is trivial at that serving size. The fiber difference is more noticeable: dates provide about 0.9 g more per 30 g. Neither, however, is as fiber-efficient per calorie as beans or many vegetables.

Piece size changes the way you eat them

One large Medjool weighs about 24 g, so 30 g is only a little more than one date. Thirty grams of raisins is dozens of small pieces. That physical difference matters because a handful can disappear without much counting.

A large date also packs plenty into one piece: about 66 calories and 16 g of sugars. Neither format automatically guarantees portion control.

What about minerals?

Both contribute potassium plus smaller amounts of iron, magnesium, and other minerals. Exact numbers shift with variety and processing. For potassium, 30 g of raisins provides roughly 225 mg and 30 g of Medjools about 209 mg—a difference of only about 16 mg.

There is no need to manufacture an overall winner from that. Choose for taste, texture, and how the food fits the meal. If fiber is your main criterion within this pair, dates have the edge; if you prefer raisins, the small calorie or potassium differences are not a compelling reason to switch.

Both are still concentrated fruit

Plain dates and raisins do not need added sugar to reach these numbers. Their naturally occurring fruit sugars become concentrated because most of the water is gone.

Using them as a visible ingredient can make portions easier to understand: 20–30 g in oatmeal, yogurt, or a nut mix adds sweetness and texture without turning the package into an endless snack. Serving size matters more than a small numerical gap between two dried fruits.

faq.question: Which has more sugar, dates or raisins?
faq.answer: Per 100 g, the reference Medjool values are about 66–67 g of sugars, compared with roughly 59 g in raisins. Values vary by variety and product.

faq.question: Which has more fiber?
faq.answer: Medjool dates: about 6.7 g per 100 g versus roughly 3.7 g in raisins. In 30 g, that is about 2.0 g versus 1.1 g.

faq.question: Which has more calories?
faq.answer: Raisins have about 299 calories per 100 g versus 277 for Medjools. In a 30-g serving, that is about 90 versus 83 calories—a small difference.
